cards.text: Friend, this one is heavy, so I'm keeping my mustache folded for a minute. Judah is in a drought, the LORD has told Jeremiah the prophet not to pray for the well-being of this people, and other prophets are promising lasting peace (Jeremiah 14:1, 11, 13). Now the LORD gives Jeremiah a word to speak, and it starts with eyes that overflow with tears, day and night.
The tears are "for the virgin daughter of my people," who has been shattered by a crushing blow. A deep, deep wound.

cards.question: In this word, going out to the country means seeing those slain by the sword. What does entering the city show?
In the word Jeremiah speaks, the prophet and the priest are the ones who stay home safe.

cards.text: Then a prayer goes up, and it opens with hard questions: "Have You rejected Judah completely? Do You despise Zion?"

cards.question: Remember those prophets promising lasting peace? The prayer says, "We hoped for ___, but no good has come."

cards.text: No peace. And the time of healing they waited for? Only terror.

cards.question: Before they ask for anything, the ones praying admit their wickedness, and even the guilt of their fathers.
The ones praying ask the LORD, for the sake of His name, not to despise them or disgrace His glorious throne. Then they ask Him to remember something and not break it. What is it?

cards.text: Then they ask if the worthless idols of the nations can bring rain. Friend, I shared a junk drawer with an expired coupon that believed in itself every single day, and it STILL never got anybody one free cookie.

cards.question: Can idols bring rain? Do the skies alone send showers? The prayer answers its own questions. Who sends the rain?

cards.text: So they put their hope in the LORD, "for You have done all these things." That's their prayer.
Now the LORD answers Jeremiah. And friend, you can feel the whole room go quiet.

cards.question: The LORD says even if two men from Israel's past stood before Him, His heart would not go out to this people. Who are they?

cards.text: Moses, Israel's leader, and Samuel, the prophet: the two best references anybody could EVER put on an application. And the LORD still says, "Send them from My presence, and let them go!"

cards.question: When the people ask Jeremiah, "Where shall we go?" the LORD gives them a safe place to run.

cards.text: Instead, each one goes where they're destined: to death, to the sword, to famine or to captivity.
The LORD will appoint four kinds of destroyers over them: the sword to kill, the dogs to drag away, and the birds of the air and beasts of the earth to devour and destroy.

cards.question: The LORD says He will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, because of what one king did in Jerusalem. Which king?

cards.text: Manasseh son of Hezekiah, king of Judah. Then the LORD asks, "Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem? Who will mourn for you?"

cards.question: The LORD tells Jerusalem that she has forsaken Him and turned her back.
So the LORD will stretch out His hand against Jerusalem and destroy her. He says, "I am weary of showing ___."

cards.text: Then a picture from harvest time: He will scatter them with a winnowing fork at the gates of the land.

cards.question: The LORD says He will bereave and destroy His people. Which ones?

answers.text: Those who have not turned from their ways
Those who listened to the false prophets
Those who fled from Jerusalem first

cards.question: The LORD says Judah's widows will be so few that you could count them on one hand.

cards.text: More numerous than the sand of the sea. And He will bring a destroyer at noon against the mothers of young men, with anguish and dismay all of a sudden.

cards.question: The mother of seven grows faint and breathes her last breath. The LORD says her sun will set while it is still day. What does that picture mean?

answers.text: She leaves the city at dusk

cards.text: And the rest, the LORD says, He will put to the sword in the presence of their enemies. That's a heavy word, friend, and you read every line of it.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 6 quotes "We hoped for ___, but no good has come.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 10 quotes "I am weary of showing ___.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The question links the prophets' promise of lasting peace (Jeremiah 14:13) to the prayer's hope for peace (14:19). The text never says the people hoped for peace because of those prophets, so the card adds a connection the text doesn't state.

rule.text: When he connects two passages, or explains what a law was for, he says only what the texts state.

findings.problem: This true or false card only tells the baker that the prophet and priest don't stay home safe. No card ever says what 14:18 actually says, that both prophet and priest travel to a land they do not know, so the baker leaves without that detail.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: Card 10 calls the idols "worthless" and adds a joke about a coupon that never delivered. The question also recasts both wrong answers as the prayer's own rhetorical questions. Together these rule out "The idols of the nations" and "The skies on their own" before the baker picks, so the card doesn't test anything.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: Jeremiah 15:2 is conditional: "If they ask you, 'Where shall we go?'". The card turns it into a statement that it happens: "When the people ask Jeremiah."

Card 1 brought in the prophets promising peace. The wrong answer "Those who listened to the false prophets" overlaps with the right answer, because people who followed the false prophets haven't turned from their ways. Jeremiah 14:16, just before the passage, also says judgment falls on the people those prophets prophesy to. A baker could argue this answer is right.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: This story card is almost word for word Jeremiah 15:3, with none of Papa Dorin's voice or framing.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.
